solution: So $\tan^{-1}\frac{Y}{X}-\ln\sqrt{X^2+Y^2}=c$; in polar form $\theta-\ln r=c$, a logarithmic spiral.

useful_results: For $\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{a_1x+b_1y+c_1}{a_2x+b_2y+c_2}$ with $a_1b_2\neq a_2b_1$, shift the origin to the intersection of the two lines (here $(1,1)$); if $a_1b_2=a_2b_1$ use $z=a_2x+b_2y$ instead.
$\frac{X\,dY-Y\,dX}{X^2+Y^2}=d\left(\tan^{-1}\frac{Y}{X}\right)$ and $\frac{X\,dX+Y\,dY}{X^2+Y^2}=\frac12\,d\ln(X^2+Y^2)$: in polar form they are $d\theta$ and $\frac{dr}{r}$.
$\int\frac{1-V}{1+V^2}dV=\tan^{-1}V-\frac12\ln(1+V^2)$.
Always carry the constant: here $c=0$ from the first point, which is easy to forget when only the second point is substituted.

questions.question: Let $y=y(x)$ be the solution curve of the differential equation $\frac{dy}{dx}+\left(\frac{2x^2+11x+13}{x^3+6x^2+11x+6}\right)y=\frac{x+3}{x+1}$, $x>-1$, which passes through the point $(0,1)$. Then $y(1)$ is equal to :
questions.key_idea: Factor $x^3+6x^2+11x+6=(x+1)(x+2)(x+3)$; partial fractions give an integrating factor that cancels against the right side.
solution: The equation is linear: $\frac{dy}{dx}+p(x)y=\frac{x+3}{x+1}$ with $p(x)=\frac{2x^2+11x+13}{(x+1)(x+2)(x+3)}$ and $\text{I.F.}=e^{\int p\,dx}$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Let $u=y\cdot\text{I.F.}$ with $u'=(x+1)(x+2)$ and integrate directly from $x=0$ to $x=1$, so no constant is solved.
solution: The integrating factor is $\mu=\frac{(x+1)^2(x+2)}{x+3}$ (from the partial fractions $p=\frac{2}{x+1}+\frac{1}{x+2}-\frac{1}{x+3}$), so $u=\mu y$ satisfies $u'=\mu\cdot\frac{x+3}{x+1}=(x+1)(x+2)$.

useful_results: Cover-up rule: for simple roots $r$ of the denominator $D$, the coefficient of $\frac{1}{x-r}$ is $\frac{N(r)}{D'(r)}$; check by comparing leading coefficients: $A+B+C=\frac{\text{lead}(N)}{\text{lead}(D)}$ when $\deg N=\deg D-1$ (here $2+1-1=2$).
$\int\frac{N}{D}\,dx$ with simple roots integrates to $\sum A_i\ln|x-r_i|$, so the integrating factor is $\prod(x-r_i)^{A_i}$ (here $(x+1)^2(x+2)(x+3)^{-1}$).
Often the integrating factor cancels the denominator on the right: here $\frac{x+3}{x+1}\cdot\mu$ simplifies to a polynomial.
Using $\mu y\Big|_{x_0}^{x_1}=\int_{x_0}^{x_1}\mu Q\,dx$ avoids finding the constant $c$.

questions.question: Let $y=y(x)$ be the solution of the differential equation $\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{4y^3+2yx^2}{3xy^2+x^3}$, $y(1)=1$. If for some $n\in\mathbb{N}$, $y(2)\in[n-1,n)$, then $n$ is equal to ______.
questions.key_idea: The right side is homogeneous of degree $0$; $y=vx$ separates the variables, and $y(2)$ is then located between consecutive integers.
solution: Integrate (numerator is the derivative of the denominator): $\ln|v^3+v|=\ln x+c$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Treat $x$ as the function of $y$ and put $x=vy$; this gives the first integral $\frac{x^4}{y(x^2+y^2)}=\text{const}$.
solution: So $4\ln v-\ln\left(1+v^2\right)+\ln y=\text{const}$, i.e. $\frac{v^4y}{1+v^2}=C$. With $v=\frac{x}{y}$ this is $\frac{x^4}{y\left(x^2+y^2\right)}=C$.
At $x=2$: $y\left(4+y^2\right)=32$, i.e. $y^3+4y=32$. As $y^3+4y$ is increasing with values $16$ at $2$ and $39$ at $3$, $2<y(2)<3$.

useful_results: A homogeneous equation $\frac{dy}{dx}=F\left(\frac{y}{x}\right)$ separates with $y=vx$: $\int\frac{dv}{F(v)-v}=\ln|x|+c$. If it looks easier, swap roles and use $x=vy$.
For $M\,dx+N\,dy=0$ with $M,N$ homogeneous of the same degree and $Mx+Ny\neq0$, $\frac{1}{Mx+Ny}$ is an integrating factor.
When $\int\frac{g'(v)}{g(v)}dv$ appears (numerator is the derivative of the denominator), the answer is $\ln|g(v)|$: here $g=v^3+v$.
To place an implicit value between integers, use monotonicity of the resulting equation and compare values at consecutive integers (intermediate value theorem): $y^3+4y$ is strictly increasing.

concepts: Formation and solution of differential equations
questions.question: Let a curve $y=y(x)$ pass through the point $(3,3)$ and the area of the region under this curve, above the $x$-axis and between the abscissae $3$ and $x\ (>3)$ be $\left(\frac{y}{X}\right)^3$. If this curve also passes through the point $\left(\alpha,6\sqrt{10}\right)$ in the first quadrant, then $\alpha$ is equal to ______.
questions.key_idea: Differentiate the area relation to get $x^4=3xyy'-3y^2$, then $t=y^2$ makes it linear.
solution: The area condition is $\int_3^{x}y\,dx=\left(\frac{y}{x}\right)^3$; differentiate with respect to $x$ to get the differential equation.
$\alpha^4-6\alpha^2-1080=0$ gives $\alpha^2=3\pm33$; the positive value is $\alpha^2=36$, so $\alpha=6$ (first quadrant, $\alpha>3$).

alternate_solutions.idea: Use $u=\frac{y}{x}$: since $xy'-y=x^2u'$, the equation becomes $x=3uu'$, an exact separable equation.

useful_results: If $A(x)=\int_a^{x}y\,dt$ is given, then $A'(x)=y(x)$; note that $A(a)=0$ is an extra condition that must be consistent with the data.
$xy'-y=x^2\frac{d}{dx}\left(\frac{y}{x}\right)$ and $yy'=\frac12\frac{d}{dx}\left(y^2\right)$: these two identities turn $y\,y'$-type equations into linear or separable ones.
Linear equation $t'+P t=Q$ with $P=-\frac{2}{x}$ has integrating factor $x^{-2}$ (since $e^{\int-2/x\,dx}=x^{-2}$).
A biquadratic in disguise: $\alpha^4-6\alpha^2-1080=0$ is a quadratic in $\alpha^2$; reject the negative root $\alpha^2=-30$.

questions.question: Suppose $y=y(x)$ be the solution curve to the differential equation $\frac{dy}{dx}-y=2-e^{-x}$ such that $\lim_{x\to\infty}y(x)$ is finite. If $a$ and $b$ are respectively the $x$- and $y$-intercepts of the tangent to the curve at $x=0$, then the value of $a-4b$ is equal to ______.
questions.key_idea: The general solution has a term $Ce^{x}$; a finite limit at $\infty$ forces $C=0$.
solution: This is possible only when $C=0$, so $y=-2+\frac{e^{-x}}{2}$.
Equation of the tangent at $\left(0,-\frac32\right)$: $y+\frac32=-\frac12(x-0)$, i.e. $x+2y=-3$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Guess the particular solution $y=c+de^{-x}$ from the right side; the homogeneous $Ce^{x}$ must vanish to keep the limit finite.
solution: The right side is $2-e^{-x}$: try $y_p=c+de^{-x}$. Then $y_p'-y_p=-de^{-x}-c-de^{-x}=-c-2de^{-x}$.
Matching with $2-e^{-x}$: $-c=2$ and $-2d=-1$, so $c=-2,\ d=\frac12$ and $y_p=-2+\frac12e^{-x}$.
General solution: $y=y_p+Ce^{x}$. As $x\to\infty$, $y_p\to-2$ but $Ce^{x}\to\pm\infty$ unless $C=0$; so $C=0$.

useful_results: For $y'-y=g(x)$ the homogeneous solution $Ce^{x}$ blows up as $x\to\infty$; a finite limit therefore selects the unique solution with $C=0$, namely $y=-\int_x^{\infty}e^{x-t}g(t)\,dt$ when this converges.
For a linear equation with right side $A+Be^{kx}$ ($k$ not equal to a root of the homogeneous exponent) try $y_p=c+de^{kx}$ (undetermined coefficients).
Tangent at $(x_0,y_0)$ with slope $m\neq0$: $x$-intercept $a=x_0-\frac{y_0}{m}$ and $y$-intercept $b=y_0-mx_0$ (here $x_0=0$ gives $a=-\frac{y_0}{m}=-3,\ b=y_0=-\frac32$).
The slope at a point can be read from the differential equation itself: $y'(0)=y(0)+2-1$.

questions.question: Let $y=y(x)$ be the solution curve of the differential equation $\sin\left(2x^2\right)\log_e\left(\tan x^2\right)dy+\left(4xy-4\sqrt2\,x\sin\left(x^2-\frac{\pi}{4}\right)\right)dx=0$, $0<x<\sqrt{\frac{\pi}{2}}$, which passes through the point $\left(\sqrt{\frac{\pi}{6}},1\right)$. Then $\left|y\left(\sqrt{\frac{\pi}{3}}\right)\right|$ is equal to ______.
questions.key_idea: Dividing by $\sin2x^2$ shows $d\left(y\ln\tan x^2\right)$, leaving $2\,\frac{dt}{t^2-1}$ with $t=\sin x^2+\cos x^2$.
solution: Since $d\left(y\ln\tan x^2\right)=\ln\left(\tan x^2\right)dy+\frac{4xy}{\sin\left(2x^2\right)}dx$, the first two terms are an exact differential.
Use $\sqrt2\sin\left(x^2-\frac{\pi}{4}\right)=\sin x^2-\cos x^2$ and $\sin2x^2=\left(\sin x^2+\cos x^2\right)^2-1$.
The equation becomes $d\left(y\ln\tan x^2\right)-\frac{4x\left(\sin x^2-\cos x^2\right)}{\left(\sin x^2+\cos x^2\right)^2-1}dx=0$.
Put $t=\sin x^2+\cos x^2$; then $dt=2x\left(\cos x^2-\sin x^2\right)dx$ and the last term is $+\frac{2\,dt}{t^2-1}$.
At $x=\sqrt{\frac{\pi}{3}}$ the value of $\sin x^2+\cos x^2$ is the same, $\frac{\sqrt3}{2}+\frac12$: $y\ln\sqrt3+\ln\frac{\sqrt3-1}{\sqrt3+3}=\ln\frac{1}{\sqrt3}+\ln\frac{\sqrt3-1}{\sqrt3+3}$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Put $u=x^2$ and integrate $d\left(y\ln\tan u\right)$ between $u=\frac{\pi}{6}$ and $\frac{\pi}{3}$; the integrand is odd about $u=\frac{\pi}{4}$, so the integral is $0$.
solution: Since $\frac{d}{du}\ln\tan u=\frac{2}{\sin2u}$, dividing by $\sin2u$ gives $\frac{d}{du}\left(y\ln\tan u\right)=g(u)$ where $g(u)=\frac{2\sqrt2\sin\left(u-\frac{\pi}{4}\right)}{\sin2u}$.
Under $u\to\frac{\pi}{2}-u$: $\sin2u$ is unchanged and $\sin\left(u-\frac{\pi}{4}\right)\to-\sin\left(u-\frac{\pi}{4}\right)$, so $g$ is odd about $\frac{\pi}{4}$.
The interval $\left[\frac{\pi}{6},\frac{\pi}{3}\right]$ is symmetric about $\frac{\pi}{4}$ and $g$ is continuous on it, so $\int g\,du=0$.

useful_results: $\frac{d}{du}\ln\tan u=\frac{1}{\sin u\cos u}=\frac{2}{\sin2u}$, so $\ln\tan u$ is the integrating factor of $y'+\frac{2}{\sin2u\,\ln\tan u}y=\dots$; $d\left(y\ln\tan u\right)=\ln\tan u\,dy+\frac{2y}{\sin2u}du$.

$\sin2u=(\sin u+\cos u)^2-1$ and $d(\sin u+\cos u)=(\cos u-\sin u)\,du$: the substitution $t=\sin u+\cos u$ rationalises integrals with $\frac{\sin u-\cos u}{\sin2u}$; $\int\frac{dt}{t^2-1}=\frac12\ln\left|\frac{t-1}{t+1}\right|$.

Reflection $u\to\frac{\pi}{2}-u$ swaps $\tan u\leftrightarrow\cot u$, fixes $\sin2u$ and flips the sign of $\sin\left(u-\frac{\pi}{4}\right)$; integrals of such odd functions over $\left[a,\frac{\pi}{2}-a\right]$ vanish.
When only $x\,dx$ and functions of $x^2$ occur, substitute $u=x^2$ first.
$\sqrt2\sin\left(u-\frac{\pi}{4}\right)=\sin u-\cos u$ (angle subtraction).
